reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
clinicalPearls: Caused by human papillomavirus, predominantly types 6 and 11, producing recurrent benign papillomata of the aerodigestive tract, most commonly the larynx
Juvenile-onset disease is thought to arise from vertical transmission around delivery from maternal genital HPV, while adult-onset disease is often sexually acquired
Progressive hoarseness or an abnormal cry is the typical presenting feature; stridor and airway obstruction develop as lesions enlarge
In a child with persistent hoarseness and stridor, RRP should be considered and can be mistaken for asthma or croup
Diagnosis rests on laryngoscopy showing exophytic, frond-like lesions, confirmed histologically with HPV typing
Disease behaviour is highly variable, ranging from a single lesion to aggressive recurrence needing frequent procedures, with HPV 11 associated with a more aggressive course
Management centres on repeated surgical debulking to preserve airway and voice while sparing normal tissue, with adjuvant medical therapies in aggressive cases
Distal spread into the trachea and lungs and rare malignant transformation are recognised complications
reference.pathophysiology: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis results from infection of respiratory epithelium by low-risk human papillomavirus, chiefly types 6 and 11. The virus infects basal epithelial cells and drives proliferation of squamous epithelium into exophytic papillomata with fibrovascular cores, showing a predilection for zones of ciliated-to-squamous epithelial transition such as the vocal folds. Latent virus in clinically normal-appearing adjacent mucosa accounts for the characteristic recurrence after removal. Host immune factors and viral type influence disease aggressiveness, and repeated growth can extend distally through the tracheobronchial tree with rare progression to squamous carcinoma.
additionalDifferentials: Subglottic stenosis or haemangioma in children
additionalInvestigations: Flexible and rigid laryngoscopy to map lesion distribution
Microlaryngoscopy under anaesthesia with biopsy for histology
Cross-sectional imaging or bronchoscopy when distal tracheobronchial or pulmonary spread is suspected
Voice assessment and serial documentation of disease burden to guide treatment intervals
redFlags: Stridor, respiratory distress or rapidly worsening airway obstruction
Rapid recurrence or bulky disease requiring increasingly frequent procedures
New pulmonary lesions suggesting distal spread
Suspicion of malignant transformation on histology or unusually rapid growth
reference.prognosis: The course is unpredictable: some patients experience spontaneous remission while others require repeated procedures over many years to maintain the airway and voice. Distal pulmonary spread and malignant transformation are uncommon but serious, and HPV vaccination is expected to reduce future incidence.
pitfalls: Mistaking childhood stridor and hoarseness for asthma or recurrent croup and delaying laryngoscopy
Aggressive deep excision causing scarring and permanent voice damage
Performing tracheostomy unnecessarily, which may promote distal seeding of disease
Neglecting surveillance for malignant change in long-standing or aggressive disease
references: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Mainstay is repeated surgical debulking that preserves normal mucosa, using a microdebrider or laser at microlaryngoscopy to maintain the airway and voice
Avoid tracheostomy wherever possible, as it risks seeding papillomata distally into the tracheobronchial tree
Add adjuvant intralesional cidofovir or systemic bevacizumab for aggressive, frequently recurrent disease
Offer HPV vaccination as an adjunct to reduce disease burden and future incidence
Undertake serial laryngoscopy and voice assessment to document burden and time repeat procedures, with surveillance for distal pulmonary spread and malignant transformation
Multidisciplinary otolaryngology care with speech-and-language voice therapy and respiratory input if pulmonary spread occurs
